identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The unnormalized attention mechanism's design, where attention weights do not depend on sibling nodes, is theoretically motivated by RST's principle that a node's presence does not signify lesser importance to its siblings.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a recursive neural network (RNN) architecture that integrates automatically-derived Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) discourse dependency trees for text categorization. A central component is a novel unnormalized attention mechanism, theoretically motivated by RST principles. The core argument posits that this integration generally enhances text categorization performance. This is empirically supported by the UNLABELED model's superior performance on four out of five diverse tasks compared to prior state-of-the-art methods. The paper meticulously analyzes the impact of model complexity, demonstrating the FULL model's advantage on very large datasets but its susceptibility to overparameterization on smaller ones. Furthermore, it establishes a positive correlation between discourse parser accuracy and classification performance and highlights the genre-dependent utility of discourse structure, noting a detrimental effect for genres significantly divergent from the parser's training data. The logical flow is robust, progressing from a clear problem statement and theoretical grounding to detailed model description, comprehensive experimental validation, and insightful analysis of influencing factors. The claims are well-linked to empirical evidence, and the overall argument is coherent.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Text categorization benefits from identifying salient passages (Section 1).
P2: Discourse structure (RST) provides cues for passage importance (Section 1).
P3: Existing discourse parsers (DPLP) can automatically derive RST-style dependency trees (Section 1, 2, 4).
Hypothesis: Integrating automatically-derived discourse structure via a recursive neural network with a novel attention mechanism will improve text categorization (Section 1, 3).
Sub-Hypothesis 1: A novel unnormalized attention mechanism, motivated by RST, will be effective (Section 1, 3.2).
Sub-Hypothesis 2: Different model variants (FULL, UNLABELED) will have varying performance characteristics based on complexity and data size (Section 3.3, 3.4).
Sub-Hypothesis 3: The benefit of discourse structure will depend on the quality of the parser and the genre (Section 1).
Method: Develop a recursive neural network (RNN) model (FULL, UNLABELED, ROOT, ADDITIVE variants) incorporating discourse dependency trees and the novel attention mechanism (Section 3).

Experiment: Evaluate model variants on five diverse text categorization datasets, comparing against SOTA baselines, including ablation studies, parser degradation study, and attention mechanism comparison (Section 4, 5, 6).
Result (C1, C2): UNLABELED model outperforms SOTA on 4/5 tasks, supporting the general benefit of discourse structure (Section 6, Table 2).
Result (C3): FULL model performs best on very large datasets (Yelp) but is overparameterized for smaller ones (Section 6, Table 2).
Result (C7): ROOT model performs poorly, implying discourse structure's benefit extends beyond a single salient EDU (Section 6, Table 2).
Result (C4): Classification accuracy positively correlates with discourse parser F1, suggesting future parser improvements will yield gains (Section 6, Figure 4).
Result (C5): Unnormalized attention empirically outperforms normalized attention, validating the design choice (Section 6).
Result (C6): Discourse structure utility is genre-dependent, with negative impact on legislative bills due to genre mismatch (Section 6).
Result (C9): DPLP generalizability across genres (reviews, debates) despite news training (Section 6).
Result (C10): Qualitative analysis shows DPLP failures and FULL model confusion with poor structure (Section 6, Figure 3c).

Conclusion: Automatically-derived discourse structure is often helpful, its benefit increases with parser accuracy, but it is genre-dependent, motivating further discourse parsing improvements, especially for new genres (Section 8).

concerns.title: Limited Explanation for FULL Model Overparameterization
concerns.description: While the paper correctly identifies that the FULL model is overparameterized for smaller datasets (C3), the explanation primarily attributes this to a higher parameter count. A deeper exploration of *why* the relation-specific composition matrices lead to overfitting or reduced performance in smaller data contexts, beyond just parameter quantity, would strengthen the analysis. comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: The paper uses the DPLP parser from Ji and Eisenstein (2014) for automatically deriving discourse structures. This work is foundational as it provides the input discourse trees for the proposed models.

The paper explicitly contrasts its novel unnormalized attention mechanism with the normalized attention mechanism proposed by Bahdanau et al. (2015), highlighting a key methodological difference motivated by RST principles.

This work is a direct predecessor, also using discourse structure for sentiment analysis. The current paper differentiates itself by learning attention weights automatically, whereas Bhatia et al. (2015) used hand-crafted weighting schemes.

Yang et al. (2016) proposed hierarchical attention networks for document classification, which serves as a key baseline for comparison, particularly for the Yelp dataset. The current paper extends this by incorporating explicit discourse structure.

The paper states its recursive neural network approach is analogous to and inspired by the use of RNNs on syntactic dependency trees, as in Socher et al. (2014). This provides a conceptual foundation for the recursive composition.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The specific combination of RST-derived dependency trees, a recursive neural network, and a theoretically-motivated unnormalized attention mechanism for general text categorization appears to be a novel integration. This novelty is separate from the methodological soundness of the implementation and evaluation.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If discourse parsing technology significantly improves in accuracy and robustness across diverse genres, the benefits of this model would likely increase across a broader range of tasks and text types.

If the model could dynamically adapt its complexity or attention mechanism based on dataset characteristics (e.g., size, genre), its applicability and performance across varied scenarios would be enhanced.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a recursive neural network (RNN) built upon automatically-derived discourse dependency trees, leveraging Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) to enhance text categorization. A key methodological contribution is a novel unnormalized attention mechanism, theoretically motivated by RST principles, which learns to weight elementary discourse units (EDUs) for salience. The paper's core argument is that this integration of discourse structure, particularly through the UNLABELED model variant, generally improves text categorization performance across a diverse set of five tasks. The methodological rigor is demonstrated through a systematic evaluation comparing FULL, UNLABELED, ROOT, and ADDITIVE model variants against strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the paper investigates the influence of external factors such as discourse parser quality and genre mismatch on the effectiveness of discourse structure, providing insights into the conditions under which this approach is most beneficial.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1: Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) provides a suitable framework for representing text organization and identifying salient content for text categorization (Assumption A1).
Premise 2: Transforming RST trees into dependency structures offers a beneficial inductive bias for neural models to discern salient text parts (Assumption A2).

Premise 3: The DPLP parser is a sufficiently accurate and state-of-the-art tool for automatically deriving discourse structures, appropriate for the tasks unless genre mismatch is noted (Assumption A3).
Premise 4: A recursive neural network architecture can effectively process these discourse dependency structures (Section 3).

Premise 5: A novel unnormalized attention mechanism, motivated by RST's principle of non-competitive sibling importance, is empirically more effective than normalized attention in this context (Assumption A4, Claim C5).
Conclusion: Integrating discourse structure via the proposed recursive neural network and unnormalized attention mechanism generally benefits text categorization (Claim C1).
Evidence for C1: The UNLABELED model variant outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on four out of five diverse text categorization tasks (Claim C2).
Evidence for C1: The FULL model shows stronger performance on very large datasets but can be overparameterized for smaller ones, indicating a nuanced benefit (Claim C3).
Evidence for C1: The ROOT model performs poorly, implying that the benefit of discourse structure extends beyond identifying a single salient EDU (Claim C7).
Conclusion: The benefit of using discourse structure for text categorization is positively correlated with the accuracy of the underlying discourse parser (Claim C4).
Evidence for C4: Experiments show that lower parsing performance (due to reduced training data for DPLP) implies lower classification accuracy (Section 6, Figure 4).
Conclusion: The utility of discourse structure for text categorization is genre-dependent (Claim C6).
Evidence for C6: The method underperforms on legislative bills, a genre significantly different from the discourse parser's training data, where discourse structure works against accuracy (Claim C6).

Evidence for C6: Despite being trained on news text, the DPLP parser still offers benefits to restaurant reviews, movie reviews, and congressional debates, demonstrating some generalizability (Claim C9).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a clear incremental advancement in text categorization by systematically integrating automatically-derived Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) based discourse structure into a recursive neural network. It builds upon existing paradigms that leverage saliency for text categorization (Ko et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2016) and prior work that applied discourse structure to sentiment analysis with hand-crafted features (Bhatia et al., 2015; Hogenboom et al., 2015). The core incremental contribution lies in the development of a recursive neural network architecture that explicitly processes discourse dependency trees, coupled with a novel unnormalized attention mechanism theoretically motivated by RST principles. The paper's strength is in its comprehensive empirical validation across diverse tasks, demonstrating that this integration generally yields performance improvements, while also meticulously analyzing the conditions (e.g., discourse parser quality, genre match) under which these incremental benefits are realized.
logical_argument_graph: Discourse structure provides cues for the relative saliency or importance of passages within a text, which can benefit text categorization (Section 1).

Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) offers a framework for representing text organization, and RST trees can be transformed into dependency structures, providing an inductive bias for neural models (Section 2, Assumption A1, A2).
Recursive neural networks are effective for composing representations from tree structures (Section 3, inspired by Socher et al., 2014).

A novel unnormalized attention mechanism, designed based on RST principles (Assumption A4), can learn to dynamically weight elementary discourse units (EDUs) within this recursive network, focusing on salient content (Section 3.2).
The proposed models (FULL and UNLABELED), which integrate discourse structure via this RNN and attention, should therefore generally benefit text categorization (Claim C1).
Empirical results show that the UNLABELED model outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on four out of five diverse text categorization tasks, validating the general benefit (Claim C2, Table 2).

The FULL model, while more complex, shows stronger performance on very large datasets but can be overparameterized for smaller ones, indicating a trade-off in complexity for incremental gains (Claim C3, Table 2).
The benefit of using discourse structure is positively correlated with the accuracy of the underlying discourse parser, highlighting the dependency on upstream components (Claim C4, Figure 4).
The proposed unnormalized attention mechanism is empirically more effective than a normalized variant, supporting its theoretically-motivated design (Claim C5).

The utility of discourse structure can be genre-dependent, with less benefit or even negative impact for genres significantly different from the discourse parser's training data, defining boundaries for the incremental utility (Claim C6).

Therefore, integrating automatically-derived discourse structure through the proposed recursive neural network and unnormalized attention mechanism offers a meaningful incremental improvement for text categorization across various genres, contingent on parser quality and genre characteristics.

strengths.title: Systematic Integration of Discourse Structure
strengths.description: The paper provides a clear and systematic methodology for integrating RST-based discourse dependency trees into a recursive neural network architecture for text categorization. This extends prior work that either used discourse for specific tasks (e.g., sentiment analysis) or relied on hand-crafted features, by offering a learned, generalizable neural approach.
evidence: Our models learn to weight the importance of a document’s sentences, based on their positions and relations in the discourse tree.

This idea of using a weighting scheme along with discourse structure is explored in prior works (Bhatia et al., 2015; Hogenboom et al., 2015), although they are manually designed, rather than learned from training data.

strengths.title: Novel Unnormalized Attention Mechanism
strengths.description: The introduction of an unnormalized attention mechanism, explicitly motivated by RST's principles regarding sibling importance, represents a meaningful incremental refinement of existing attention models. Empirical validation against a normalized variant supports its effectiveness in this specific context.
evidence: We introduce a new, unnormalized attention mechanism to this end.

Our attention mechanism differs from prior work (Bahdanau et al., 2015), in which attention weights are normalized to sum to one across competing candidates for attention. Here, ↵_i,j does not depend on node i’s other children. This is motivated by RST, in which the presence of a node does not signify lesser importance to its siblings.
This variant of the FULL model [with normalized attention] achieves 70.3% accuracy, giving empirical support to our theoretically-motivated design decision not to normalize attention.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript introduces a novel approach to text categorization by integrating Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) derived discourse structures with a recursive neural network. The core innovation lies in a newly proposed *unnormalized attention mechanism*, which is theoretically motivated by RST's principles regarding the non-competitive nature of sibling nodes in a discourse tree. This design choice explicitly diverges from common normalized attention mechanisms found in prior work (e.g., Bahdanau et al., 2015). The paper empirically validates this unconventional attention mechanism and demonstrates that the proposed models, particularly the UNLABELED variant, generally outperform state-of-the-art methods across four out of five diverse text categorization tasks. Furthermore, the work provides a nuanced analysis of factors influencing performance, such as the quality of the underlying discourse parser and the genre-dependency of discourse utility, highlighting conditions under which the approach is most effective or may face limitations.
logical_argument_graph: Text categorization can benefit from identifying salient passages (Ko et al., 2004; Yessenalina et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2016).
Discourse structure (RST) provides cues for importance and has shown promise in sentiment analysis with hand-crafted schemes (Bhatia et al., 2015; Hogenboom et al., 2015).
Hypothesis: Integrating automatically-derived discourse structure via a recursive neural network with a novel attention mechanism will generally benefit text categorization.
Proposed Model: A recursive neural network built on RST-derived dependency trees, using a bidirectional LSTM for EDU representations.

Key Innovation: An *unnormalized attention mechanism* (Equation 2) is introduced, motivated by RST's principle that a node's presence does not signify lesser importance to its siblings, unlike normalized attention in other contexts (Bahdanau et al., 2015).
Model Variants: FULL (relation-specific composition matrices) and UNLABELED (only tree structure, no relations, fewer parameters) are developed.
Baselines: ROOT (only root EDU) and ADDITIVE (average of all EDUs, discourse-ignorant) are included for comparison.
Experimental Setup: Models are evaluated on five diverse text categorization datasets, using DPLP (Ji and Eisenstein, 2014) for discourse parsing.
Result 1 (C1, C2): Variants of the model (especially UNLABELED) generally outperform prior work on four out of five tasks, demonstrating benefit from discourse structure.
Result 2 (C3): The FULL model performs best on very large datasets (Yelp) but can be overparameterized for smaller ones, where UNLABELED or even ADDITIVE might be better.
Result 3 (C7): The ROOT model performs poorly, indicating that the full discourse structure, not just a single salient EDU, is crucial.
Result 4 (C4): Benefit of discourse structure is positively correlated with the accuracy of the underlying discourse parser (demonstrated by parser degradation experiments).
Result 5 (C5): The proposed unnormalized attention mechanism is empirically more effective than a normalized variant, supporting its theoretical motivation.

Result 6 (C6, C9): The utility of discourse structure is genre-dependent; it helps for reviews and debates despite parser training on news, but can hurt for significantly different genres like legislative bills, where discourse conventions diverge.

Conclusion: Automatically-derived discourse structure is often helpful, its benefit increases with parser accuracy, but genre mismatch can negate its utility. The novel unnormalized attention mechanism is effective.

concerns.title: Overparameterization Explanation for FULL Model
concerns.description: The paper identifies that the FULL model is 'overparameterized for the smaller datasets' (C3), leading to worse performance than the UNLABELED or even ADDITIVE models. While this is a plausible explanation, the discussion could benefit from a more detailed analysis of *why* the relation-specific matrices lead to such significant overparameterization in practice for smaller datasets, perhaps with a breakdown of parameter counts for each component or a more formal analysis of model capacity relative to data size.
evidence: In the case of the very large Yelp dataset, our FULL model (line 9) gives even stronger performance, but not elsewhere, suggesting that it is overparameterized for the smaller datasets.
Indeed, on the MFC and Movies tasks, the discourse-ignorant ADDITIVE outperforms the FULL model.
On these datasets, the selected FULL model had nearly 20 times as many parameters as the UNLABELED model, which in turn had twice as many parameters as the ADDITIVE.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a more in-depth discussion or analysis of the parameter count differences between the FULL and UNLABELED models, explicitly linking the number of relation types and matrix sizes to the observed overparameterization. This could include a sensitivity analysis or a theoretical argument for why this specific parameter increase is detrimental for smaller datasets.

alternative_interpretations: The 'overparameterization' of the FULL model on smaller datasets (C3) could also be interpreted as a lack of sufficient training data to learn the more complex relation-specific composition matrices effectively, rather than solely an issue of parameter count. With more data, the FULL model might consistently outperform UNLABELED.

The genre-dependent utility of discourse structure (C6) might not solely be due to the DPLP parser's training data mismatch. It could also reflect inherent differences in the *relevance* of RST-defined discourse relations for categorization in certain genres (e.g., legislative bills might rely more on specific keywords or legal structures than rhetorical flow).

The empirical superiority of the unnormalized attention mechanism (C5) could be context-specific to RST dependency trees and the chosen tasks. It's possible that for other tree structures or NLP tasks, a normalized attention mechanism might prove more effective or necessary.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The unnormalized attention mechanism, theoretically motivated by RST's non-competitive sibling principle, represents a novel architectural choice. Its divergence from standard normalized attention (Bahdanau et al., 2015) is a deliberate design decision, not a methodological flaw, and is empirically validated. The overparameterization of the FULL model for smaller datasets is a practical limitation related to model capacity and data size, which is a methodological concern, not a direct indictment of the novelty of integrating RST.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If discourse parsers were significantly more accurate and robust across a wider range of genres, the benefits of integrating discourse structure would likely be more pronounced and consistent across all tasks.

If larger training datasets were available for all categorization tasks, the FULL model, with its higher parameter count and ability to learn relation-specific compositions, might consistently outperform the UNLABELED model.

If the underlying theoretical assumptions of RST regarding discourse relations and salience were universally applicable and accurately captured by automatic parsers for all text genres, the model's performance would be less genre-dependent.

If the attention mechanism or composition functions were further refined to be more robust to noisy or imperfect discourse parses, the model's performance could improve, especially in challenging genres.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The integration of discourse structure into neural networks for text categorization builds upon existing work that leverages saliency (Ko et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2016) and prior applications of discourse to sentiment analysis (Bhatia et al., 2015). The recursive neural network structure itself is inspired by prior work on syntactic dependency trees (Socher et al., 2014). The primary incremental novelty lies in the systematic application of a recursive neural network to automatically-derived RST dependency trees and the specific design of the unnormalized attention mechanism within this context.

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The paper introduces a recursive neural network (RNN) architecture that integrates automatically-derived Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) discourse dependency trees for text categorization. A central component is a novel unnormalized attention mechanism, theoretically motivated by RST principles. The core argument posits that this integration generally enhances text categorization performance, empirically supported by the UNLABELED model's superior performance on four out of five diverse tasks compared to prior state-of-the-art methods. The work meticulously analyzes the impact of model complexity, demonstrating the FULL model's advantage on very large datasets but its susceptibility to overparameterization on smaller ones. Furthermore, it establishes a positive correlation between discourse parser accuracy and classification performance and highlights the genre-dependent utility of discourse structure, noting a detrimental effect for genres significantly divergent from the parser's training data.

Strengths:
- The systematic integration of RST-based discourse dependency trees into a recursive neural network provides a clear methodology for leveraging linguistic structure in text categorization.
- The introduction of a novel unnormalized attention mechanism, explicitly motivated by RST principles, represents a theoretically grounded and empirically validated architectural refinement.
- The experimental evaluation is comprehensive and rigorous, covering five diverse text categorization datasets, multiple model variants, and insightful ablation studies.
- The paper provides valuable analysis on the impact of external factors such as discourse parser quality and genre characteristics, deepening the understanding of when and why discourse structure is beneficial or detrimental.
- Detailed information on preprocessing, word embedding strategies, and hyperparameter optimization, along with an implementation link, enhances reproducibility.

Limitations:
- The FULL model's overparameterization on smaller datasets is noted, but a deeper analytical explanation of *why* relation-specific composition matrices lead to overfitting or reduced performance beyond just parameter quantity is lacking.
- The qualitative analysis of failure modes, particularly for the legislative bills dataset and the example in Figure 3(c), is somewhat brief and interpretive, lacking a more mechanistic explanation of how discourse parsing errors propagate to model confusion.
- The generalizability of the parser degradation analysis, which correlates parser quality with classification accuracy, is primarily demonstrated on a single dataset (Yelp), limiting universal claims.
- The model's performance is heavily reliant on the accuracy and generalizability of the upstream DPLP discourse parser, meaning incremental gains are bounded by current parsing technology and susceptible to errors, especially for out-of-domain genres.

Open Questions:
- Could the authors provide a more detailed breakdown of the specific discourse parsing errors in Figure 3(c) and a mechanistic explanation of how these errors propagate through the recursive neural network to confuse the attention mechanism, rather than a general statement of 'confusion'?
- To strengthen the generalizability of the parser degradation analysis, could the authors extend this experiment to at least one additional diverse dataset (e.g., MFC or Debates) to assess the robustness of the observed correlation between parser quality and classification performance?
- Can the authors provide a more in-depth discussion or analysis of the parameter count differences between the FULL and UNLABELED models, explicitly linking the number of relation types and matrix sizes to the observed overparameterization for smaller datasets?
- What is the specific methodological justification for choosing bidirectional LSTMs for EDU representation in this discourse context, beyond general effectiveness, and how might alternative architectures impact performance?

- The paper explicitly states the use of DPLP (Ji and Eisenstein, 2014) as the discourse parser, its training data (WSJ), and its greedy decoding algorithm.
- Details on preprocessing steps, word embedding strategies (GloVe vs. trained), and hyperparameter optimization methods (grid search, development sets/cross-validation) are provided.
- The theoretical motivation for the novel unnormalized attention mechanism is clearly articulated, contrasting it with prior normalized approaches.
- Limitations regarding the certainty of extrapolation from the discourse parser degradation experiment are explicitly acknowledged.

Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?

Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
